# What Is a Sales Compensation Plan?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-sales-compensation-plan/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A sales compensation plan is the written set of rules that turns a seller's results into pay. Its main parts are target pay, the split between base and incentive, the upside for over-performance, the measures, the quota and the payout curve. Survey data from WorldatWork and the Alexander Group shows typical choices, and field research shows that design changes behaviour in predictable ways.

A sales compensation plan is the written set of rules that decides how a seller's results turn into pay. It fixes target earnings, the split between base salary and incentive, the upside available for over-performance, which results count, the quota, and how payout rises or falls with attainment. Sellers read the plan more closely than any strategy document, so the plan is where strategy either reaches the field or does not.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What a sales compensation plan means

Every plan answers the same questions.

| Component | Question it answers | Common practice in the survey data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Target total compensation | What does a seller earn at 100% of quota? | Set from the labour market for the role |
| Pay mix | How much is base, how much at risk? | 54/46 for field new-account sellers; 66/34 for first-line managers (WorldatWork, 2022) |
| Upside (leverage ratio) | What can a top performer earn? | Often three times the target incentive (Alexander Group) |
| Measures | Which results count? | Two or three measures in 71% of plans |
| Quota | What result earns target pay? | See [Sales Capacity and Quota Setting](https://lowob.com/research/sales-capacity-and-quota-setting/) |
| Payout curve | How does pay change with attainment? | Thresholds in about 60% of plans; regressive rates above a level in 45% |
| Caps and windfall rules | What happens on unusually large deals? | Caps in 50%; mega-deal policies in 46% |
| Crediting rules | Who gets credit when several people touch a deal? | Written split rules, decided before the deal |

The Alexander Group defines mix as the relationship between base salary and the incentive part of target pay, written as two parts of 100%. It defines the leverage ratio as the total incentive available for outstanding performance, expressed as a multiple of the target incentive.

## How it works

A worked example from the Alexander Group shows how the numbers fit.

| Performance | Base | Incentive | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Target pay, 70/30 mix | $70,000 | $30,000 | $100,000 |
| Poor performer | $70,000 | $0 | $70,000 |
| At quota | $70,000 | $30,000 | $100,000 |
| Top performer, 90th percentile, 3x | $70,000 | $90,000 | $160,000 |

The firm suggests that in a well-designed uncapped plan, fewer than 10% of sellers should earn above the upper upside amount. If many more do, the quota or the payout curve is the first place to look.

Mix follows the sale. The Alexander Group describes higher-base plans for complex technical sales, long cycles and government buyers. WorldatWork's data shows the same pattern: field sellers chasing new accounts carry more pay at risk than sellers managing current customers, at 46% against 41%.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### The plan changes behaviour

Thomas Steenburgh and Michael Ahearne's research divides sales forces into laggards, core performers and stars. In field data from a Fortune 500 company, replacing quarterly bonuses with annual ones cut laggards' revenue by about 10%. Ahearne's experiment found tiered targets pushed core performers to sell more. Caps led stars to stop selling once they hit target, and Steenburgh recommends higher commission rates that apply only above target.

### Quota realism decides whether the plan pays

The 2023 Alexander Group survey, reported by WorldatWork, found a gap of 18 points between planned and projected attainment. A plan built on a quota most sellers miss pays out less than designed, and the incentive stops motivating. [Sales Capacity and Quota Setting](https://lowob.com/research/sales-capacity-and-quota-setting/) covers how to build quota from ramp and attainment.

### Profit and price belong in the plan

The same survey found 71% of respondents included profitability in sales manager or seller plans, mostly as a modifier. A plan that pays on bookings alone rewards discounting. Linking pay to realised price is one of the controls set out in [Discount Governance](https://lowob.com/research/discount-governance/).

> Sellers follow the plan, not the strategy deck. If the two disagree, the plan wins.

## How to check your plan

| Test | Warning sign |
| --- | --- |
| Can a seller calculate their own pay from the plan document? | Payouts need a finance query |
| Do measures match the strategy for the year? | Strategy says retention; plan pays only new bookings |
| Is renewal and expansion ownership stated? | Two roles both expect credit; see [Renewals and Expansion](https://lowob.com/research/renewals-and-expansion/) |
| Are crediting splits written before deals close? | Splits are negotiated after signature |
| How many sellers exceeded the upside last year? | Far more or far fewer than about one in ten |

In **lowob**'s model the plan is one of the yearly decisions worth recording, with its reasoning, owner and expected attainment, and graded at year end. Credit disputes and windfall rulings are smaller decisions of the same kind. An agent can draft commission statements and flag disputes at autonomy level 1 or 2. Who gets paid what stays with a person.

## lowob takeaways

- **The plan is a set of rules.** Mix, upside, measures, quota, curve and crediting all need writing down.
- **Design shapes effort.** Caps, bonus timing and tiers change what each group of sellers does.
- **Quota realism comes first.** A plan built on unreachable quotas stops motivating.
- **Record rulings.** Splits and windfall decisions set precedent for the next dispute.
